bib.title: RankZephyr: Effective and Robust Zero-Shot Listwise Reranking is a Breeze!

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "RankZephyr: Effective and Robust Zero-Shot Listwise Reranking is a Breeze!", Ronak Pradeep, Sahel Sharifymoghaddam, Jimmy Lin (Waterloo), arXiv:2312.02724v1 [cs.IR], preprint, 5 Dec 2023.

COVERAGE: 58,476 of 58,476 chars read (all of it, including references). The paper has no appendix and no Limitations section; limits are stated inline in Sections 5 and 6. Figures were not extracted. Only the Fig 1 prompt text appears in the extraction.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: A 7B open model (Zephyr-beta, distilled from RankGPT4) matches or beats RankGPT4 as a listwise reranker on in-domain TREC DL19/DL20 (SPLADE++ ED top-100).
  number: nDCG@10 DL19 0.7816 vs 0.7464, DL20 0.8159 vs 0.7076; with 3 passes, 0.7855 / 0.8255
  setup: MS MARCO v1; SPLADE++ ED top-100; sliding window 20/stride 10; RankGPT4 averaged over 3 runs.
  quote: "(4) RankGPT4 SPLADE++ ED 100 0.7464 0.7076 0.7721 0.7175 0.5327 0.8792 ... (7) RankZephyr SPLADE++ ED 100 0.7816 0.8159 0.7598 0.6692 0.5060 0.8535 (8) RankZephyrρ SPLADE++ ED 100 0.7855 0.8255 0.7688 0.6628 0.5107 0.8566"
  where: Table 1, ~char 15,000
- Claim: Out of domain, RankZephyr trails RankGPT4 when reranking strong SPLADE++ candidates. The authors say more work is needed.
  number: DL22 0.6692 vs 0.7175; NEWS 0.5060 vs 0.5327; COVID 0.8535 vs 0.8792 (Table 1)
  setup: same as above; MS MARCO v2 (DL21, DL22) and BEIR NEWS and COVID were never seen in training.
  quote: "However, on these datasets, our models still underperform their RankGPT4 teacher when rerank-ing SPLADE++ ED output."
  where: Section 5
  Their two guesses: the 4096-token training context versus GPT-4's 8192, and 2-4 points lower Judged@10.
- Claim: With weak BM25 candidates, RankZephyrρ beats RankGPT4 on 3 of 4 out-of-domain sets. It loses on COVID, which they attribute to GPT-4's scientific knowledge.
  number: DL21 0.7114 vs 0.7073; DL22 0.5164 vs 0.5078; NEWS 0.5333 vs 0.5069; COVID 0.8377 vs 0.8471
  setup: BM25 top-100, nDCG@10
  quote: "(3) RankGPT4 BM25 100 0.7073 0.5078 0.5069 0.8471 ... (5) RankZephyrρ BM25 100 0.7114 0.5164 0.5333 0.8377"
  where: Table 6
- Claim: Progressive reranking (feeding each pass's output into the next, 3 passes) generally helps a little. It is not uniform: DL22 and COVID were mixed.
  number: DL19 0.7816 -> 0.7855; DL20 0.8159 -> 0.8255 (Table 1)
  setup: "RankZephyrρ" = same model reranking the list 3 times, taken from RankVicuna's finding of up to 3 passes.
  quote: "progressive reranking, shown in row (8), generally improves effectiveness compared to the single-pass counterpart, row (7)"
  where: Section 5
- Claim: A better first stage gives better reranking, with diminishing returns. BM25 gains are large and SPLADE++ gains are small. A first stage with higher MAP@100 (RepLLaMA) did not give better reranked results than SPLADE++ ED.
  number: BM25 +45%-55%; SPLADE++ +7%-20%
  setup: DL19/DL20, nDCG@10 and MAP@100 and other metrics, top-100 candidates.
  quote: "while reranking the top 100 BM25 candidates with RankZephyr results in a 45%–55% im-provement in effectiveness across various metrics, the improvement is more modest with SPLADE++ ED, ranging from 7%–20% for the same metrics."
  where: Section 6.3
  BM25 alone is 0.5058 / 0.4796 nDCG@10 (Table 5). RankZephyr over BM25 top-100 gives 0.7420 / 0.7086.
- Claim: Reranking top-100 beats top-20 in most cases (the pool matters), but not always.
  number: BM25 DL19 0.6489 (top-20) vs 0.7420 (top-100); on DL19 with dense retrievers, top-20 was better, e.g. RepLLaMA 0.7848 vs 0.7660
  setup: Table 5, RankZephyr
  quote: "exceptions are noted in the DL19 dataset with dense retrievers, where rerank-ing the top 20 yields better nDCG@10 scores than reranking the top 100. This is partially attributable to the 3% difference in the percentage of the top 10 results judged."
  where: Section 6.3
- Claim: Robustness to input order. RankGPT3.5 degrades heavily when the candidate list is shuffled. RankZephyr barely does.
  number: RankGPT3.5 SPLADE++ DL19 0.7504 -> 0.6028 shuffled. RankZephyr SPLADE++ DL19 0.7816 -> 0.7670, DL20 0.8159 -> 0.7910.
  setup: top-100, six shuffled orderings, 99% CIs.
  quote: "(1d) RankGPT3.5 Shuf. SPLADE++ ED 100 0.6028 ±0.007 ... (2d) RankZephyr Shuf. SPLADE++ ED 100 0.7670 ±0.011"
  where: Table 7, Section 6.4
- Claim: Training on variable window sizes (p ≤ 20 passages, 3 random subsets of each 20) makes malformed outputs vanish at small windows. Fixed-20 training breaks at window 10.
  number: window 10/5 OK rate 38.74% (fixed training) vs 100.00% (variable); RankGPT4 at 20/10 is 95.11% OK
  setup: BM25 top-100, sliding window x/y
  quote: "(2b) RankZephyr × 10/5 38.74% 0.98% 12.05% 48.24%" and "(3b) RankZephyr ✓ 10/5 100.00% 0.00% 0.00% 0.00%"
  where: Table 3
  RankGPT4 failures are mostly refusals to rank. RankZephyr output is deterministic.
- Claim: A larger window helps most when first-stage candidates are weak. Listwise can promote several buried relevant documents at once, and pairwise can't.
  number: BM25 DL19 variable-trained, window 2/1: 0.5836; 10/5: 0.7015; 20/10: 0.7420
  setup: Table 4 (nDCG@10)
  quote: "listwise methods, with larger context windows, excel at concurrently promoting several poorly ranked relevant documents into higher positions."
  where: Section 6.2
- Claim: On the uncontaminated NovelEval-2306, RankZephyr beats RankGPT4 on nDCG@1 but not on nDCG@5 or nDCG@10.
  number: nDCG@1 0.9286 vs 0.8571; nDCG@10 0.8934 vs 0.9045
  setup: 21 queries, Google Search top-20, single window with no progressive pass, graded 0-2.
  quote: "(4) RankGPT4 0.8571 0.8749 0.9045 (5) RankZephyr 0.9286 0.8615 0.8934"
  where: Table 8
  The authors say this suggests RankZephyr is a good alternative in a RAG setting where only the top candidate is used. The sample is very small.
- Claim: Training recipe. Stage 1 is distillation from RankGPT3.5 on 100K MS MARCO queries (BM25 top-20). Stage 2 is RankGPT4 on 5K random queries with ADA2 orderings. Stage 2 takes about a tenth of the effort. The cost of full GPT-4 data is estimated at over $10K.
  number: 3 epochs, batch size 64, learning rate 5e-6, about 40 hours on 8x RTX A6000
  quote: "Due to the prohibitive cost of generating high-quality RankGPT4 training data for the entire set of 100K queries, estimated at over $10K USD, we limited our experimentation to a subset of no more than 5K queries."
  where: Sections 3.2-3.3
- Claim: Training-data ablations (DL19/DL20 nDCG@10, Table 2). ADA2 input orderings beat BM25 orderings on DL20. Discriminative query sampling is marginally worse than random. Combining both gives no gain. The authors conclude that a general query distribution matters more than covering tail queries.
  number: 3a BM25 DL20 0.7503 vs 4a ADA2 DL20 0.7762
  quote: "exposing the model to a general distribution of queries and teacher reorderings is important."
  where: Section 6.1
- Claim: RankZephyr beats the pointwise fine-tuned RankLLaMA-13B without human labels.
  number: DL19 0.7816 vs 0.7567; DL20 0.8159 vs 0.7748
  quote: "RankZephyr improves over the highly effective pointwise RankLLaMA-13B, despite not requir-ing human labels and having only 7B parameters"
  where: Section 5, Table 1 row 3
  Note this compares different first stages (RepLLaMA vs SPLADE++). Reranking the RepLLaMA candidate set also still wins (Table 5 row 3c).
- Claim: Judgment pools. These listwise runs were not in the TREC pools, so the reported scores are lower bounds.
  number: Judged@10 0.942 (DL19), 0.983 (DL20)
  quote: "the nDCG@10 scores reported here represent a lower bound of what such a run would score if part of the judgment pool."
  where: Section 5
- Claim: Inference recipe. Window 20, stride 10, over the top 100, with no extra model-specific tuning. The prompt replaces "[n]" inside passages with "(n)" so it doesn't confuse the identifier format. Output format is "[4] > [2]".
  quote: "we maintained the same parameters as RankGPT (window size of 20, stride of 10)"
  where: Section 3.4

LIMITS
- Authors concede the out-of-domain gap to RankGPT4 on strong first stages. They also note the 4096 context limit and lower Judged@10.
- Only English. All tests are passage ranking: MS MARCO v1/v2, two BEIR sets, and NovelEval with 21 queries. There is no latency or cost measurement of sliding-window reranking and no comparison with cross-encoders (monoT5 appears only on NovelEval).
- Teacher and baseline are gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4 (2023). These models are dated.
- RankGPT results are averaged over 3 or 6 runs because they are non-deterministic.
- The RepLLaMA vs SPLADE reranking anomaly is only partly explained ("likely additional factors").
- Progressive reranking costs 3x the inference calls. The paper does not report this cost.

BUILDS ON
- RankGPT (Sun et al., 2023): prompt, sliding window, NovelEval
- RankVicuna (Pradeep et al., 2023b): two-stage distillation, data augmentation by shuffling, progressive reranking, malformed-output taxonomy
- LRL (Ma et al., 2023b)
- Zephyr-beta (Tunstall et al., 2023), on Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023)
- NEFTune (Jain et al., 2023)
- RankLLaMA/RepLLaMA (Ma et al., 2023a)
- Permutation Self-Consistency (Tang et al., 2023)
- monoBERT (Nogueira and Cho, 2019)
- duoBERT (Nogueira et al., 2019), duoT5 (Pradeep et al., 2021b)
- Pointwise/pairwise/listwise lineage: Gao et al., 2021; Zhuang et al., 2022
- Multi-stage design: Matveeva et al., 2006; Cambazoglu et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011
- Data: MS MARCO (Bajaj et al., 2016), BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021), TREC DL 2019-2022

CODE
Prompt (Figure 1, p. 3):
<|system|> You are RankLLM, an intelligent assistant that can rank passages based on their relevancy to the query.
<|user|> I will provide you with {num} passages, each indicated by a numerical identifier []. Rank the passages based on their relevance to the search query: {query}. [1] {passage 1} ... Search Query: {query}. Rank the {num} passages above based on their relevance to the search query. All the passages should be included and listed using identifiers, in descending order of relevance. The output format should be [] > [], e.g., [4] > [2]. Only respond with the ranking results, do not say any word or explain.
<|assistant|> [9] > [4] > [20] > ... > [13]
Code repository: https://github.com/castorini/rank_llm

FIGURES: Fig 1 only (the prompt, above). It explains the output format faster than prose. The captions script was not run.

PROBLEMS: None serious. Table text is flattened, and column headers in Tables 1 and 2 are interleaved. I matched columns by order against the row values. The text refers to a "row (9)" in Table 1 that doesn't exist (it likely means row 8). Table 3 RankGPT4 "Repetition" reads "0.19" with no % sign. No embedded instructions found.
